'''Frances V. Spence''' ({{nee}} Bilas; March 2, 1922 – July 18, 2012<ref>{{cite web|title=Frances B. Spence|url=http://www.genealogybank.com/gbnk/ssdi/doc/news/1402B2B3A308C000|publisher=genealogybank|access-date=December 1, 2013}}{{subscription required}}</ref>) was an American physicist and computer scientist. She was one of the original programmers for the [[ENIAC]] (the first electronic digital computer). She is considered one of the first computer programmers in history.<ref name="Frances Spence"/>

The other five ENIAC programmers were [[Betty Holberton]], [[Ruth Teitelbaum]], [[Kathleen Antonelli]], [[Marlyn Meltzer]], and [[Jean Bartik]].

==Early life==
She was born '''Frances V. Bilas''' in [[Philadelphia, Pennsylvania|Philadelphia]] in 1922 and was the second of five sisters.<ref name="Frances Spence">{{cite web|title=Frances V. Spence profile|url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Frances_Spence|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141030220414/http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Frances_Spence|url-status=dead|archive-date=2014-10-30|work=Frances Spence|publisher=IEEE Global History Network|access-date=October 30, 2014}}</ref> Her parents both held jobs in the education sector, her father as an engineer for the Philadelphia Public School System and her mother as a teacher.<ref name="Frances Spence" />

Bilas attended the South Philadelphia High School for Girls and graduated in 1938.<ref name="Frances Spence" /> She originally attended [[Temple University]], but switched to [[Chestnut Hill College]] after being awarded a scholarship. She majored in mathematics with a minor in physics and graduated in 1942. While there, she met [[Kathleen Antonelli]], who later also became an [[ENIAC]] programmer.{{cn|date=August 2022}}

==Personal life==
In 1947, she married Homer W. Spence, an Army electrical engineer from the [[Aberdeen Proving Grounds]] who had been assigned to the ENIAC project and later became head of the Computer Research Branch. They had three sons (Joseph, Richard, and William).

Frances Spence had continued working on the ENIAC in the years after the war, but shortly after her marriage, she resigned to raise a family.<ref name="Frances Spence" /> She died in 2012 and is buried at the Cemetery of the Holy Rood in [[Westbury, New York|Westbury, Nassau County, New York]], USA.

==ENIAC career==
{{Moresources|section|date=August 2022}}
[[File:Two women operating ENIAC (full resolution).jpg|right|thumbnail|upright=1.5|Programmers [[Betty Jean Jennings]] (left) and Frances Bilas (right) operate the ENIAC's main control panel.]]
The ENIAC project was a classified project by the [[US Army]] to construct the first all-electronic digital computer.<ref name="Frances Spence" /> While its hardware was primarily built by a team of men,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/blogs/alltechconsidered/2014/10/06/345799830/the-forgotten-female-programmers-who-created-modern-tech/|title=The Forgotten Female Programmers Who Created Modern Tech|website=NPR.org|publisher=NPR|access-date=November 1, 2014}}</ref> its computational development was led by a team of six programmers (called "[[computer (job description)|Computers]]"), all women from similar backgrounds as Spence. Despite her importance as one of the original programmers of the ENIAC, the role that she and the other female programmers took on was largely downplayed at the time due to the stigma that women were not interested in technology.{{cn|date=August 2022}}

Photos of the women working on the computer often went without credit in newspapers at the time, and when the ENIAC was completed and unveiled to the public on February 15, 1946, the US Army failed to mention the names of the female programmers who had programmed the machine to run such sophisticated calculations.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/computinghistory/eniac.html|title=Programming the ENIAC|publisher=Columbia University|access-date=November 2, 2014}}</ref> This further contributed to the perceived disconnect between women and computing.{{cn|date=August 2022}}

Frances Bilas and the other women were originally hired by the [[University of Pennsylvania]]'s [[Moore School of Engineering]] to create the ENIAC, which was needed to compute [[ballistics]] trajectories as part of a team of eighty women. The Moore School of Engineering was funded by the US Army, and at the time they were hiring female programmers in particular due to the fact that many young American men were fighting overseas in [[World War II]].<ref name="Frances Spence" /> 

Bilas and her Chestnut Hill College classmate [[Kathleen Antonelli]] were part of a smaller team within the ENIAC team. In addition to their larger programming duties, they were also assigned to the operation of an analog computing machine known as a [[Differential Analyzer]], which was used to calculate ballistics equations (something which all the women on the ENIAC team were proficient at doing by hand). When the War ended, both Spence and Antonelli continued working with the ENIAC and they collaborated with other leading mathematicians.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.linuxchix.org/book/export/html/968/|title=Famous Women in Computing|publisher=LinuxChix Magazine|access-date=November 1, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402053717/http://www.linuxchix.org/book/export/html/968|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Legacy==
In 1997, Spence was inducted into the [[WITI Hall of Fame|Women in Technology International Hall of Fame]],<ref name="Hall of fame">{{cite web|title=WITI Hall of Fame|url=http://www.witi.com/center/witimuseum/halloffame/298369/ENIAC-Programmers-Kathleen-McNulty,-Mauchly-Antonelli,-Jean-Jennings-Bartik,-Frances-Synder-Holber-Marlyn-Wescoff-Meltzer,-Frances-Bilas-Spence-and-Ruth-Lichterman-Teitelbaum/|work=WITI - Women in Technology International|access-date=October 27, 2013}}</ref> along with the other original ENIAC programmers. Their work paved the way for the electronic computers of the future, and their innovation kick-started the rise of electronic computing and computer programming in the Post-World War II era.<ref name="The UNIVAC and the Legacy of the ENIAC">{{cite web|title=Penn Library Exhibitions|url=http://www.library.upenn.edu/exhibits/rbm/mauchly/jwm11.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030326204327/http://www.library.upenn.edu/exhibits/rbm/mauchly/jwm11.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 26, 2003|work=University of Pennsylvania|publisher=Penn Library|access-date=January 15, 2017}}</ref>

In 2010, a documentary called, "''[[Top Secret Rosies: The Female "Computers" of WWII]]''" was released.  The film centered around in-depth interviews of three of the six women programmers, focusing on the commendable patriotic contributions they made during World War II.{{Listen|type=speech|pos=right|filename=The ENIAC Programmers (As Told By U.S. Chief Technology Officer Megan Smith).ogg|title=The ENIAC Programmers (As Told By U.S. Chief Technology Officer Megan Smith)|description= }}The ENIAC team is the inspiration behind the award-winning 2013 documentary ''The Computers''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=ENIAC Programmers Project - Documentary Info|url=http://eniacprogrammers.org/documentary-info/|website=ENIAC Programmers Project|language=en-US|access-date=2020-05-24}}</ref> This documentary, created by Kathy Kleiman and the ENIAC Programmers Project, combines actual footage of the ENIAC team from the 1940s with interviews with the female team members as they reflect on their time working together on the ENIAC.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://eniacprogrammers.org/documentary|title=The Computers Documentary|publisher=The ENIAC Programmers Project|access-date=November 2, 2014}}</ref> It is the first documentary of a series of three, and parts two and three will be entitled ''The Coders'' and ''The Future-Maker'', respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://readwrite.com/2014/09/06/female-programmers-remembered-eniac-programmers|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140908075503/http://readwrite.com/2014/09/06/female-programmers-remembered-eniac-programmers|url-status=usurped|archive-date=September 8, 2014|title=History's Female Programmers Will No Longer Be Forgotten|date=6 September 2014|publisher=ReadWrite|access-date=November 2, 2014}}</ref>
